messages.content: I want to learn Hindi but the script scares me. Is Devanagari an alphabet like English?

Not quite — and the difference actually makes it *more* regular than English, not less. Devanagari is an **abugida**: the basic unit is not a lone consonant but a consonant with a built-in vowel.

Every consonant letter carries an inherent **a** sound (a short "uh"):

- क = **ka** (not just "k")
- म = **ma**
- त = **ta**
- प = **pa**

So कमल is read **kamal** (lotus) straight off the page — no guessing which vowel goes where, unlike English "read" vs "read."

To change the vowel, you don't add a separate letter; you attach a small sign called a **mātrā** to the consonant: का **kā**, कि **ki**, की **kī**. To remove the vowel entirely, a slash underneath called the **halant** kills it: क् = bare **k**.

The honest pitch: Devanagari is almost perfectly phonetic. One symbol, one sound, nearly every time. English spelling is the chaotic one in this comparison — Hindi speakers learning English have the harder script problem.
What's the line on top of Hindi words? Do the letters really hang from it?

Yes — that line is the **śirorekhā** (शिरोरेखा, literally "head-line"), and letters genuinely hang below it rather than sitting on a baseline like English. When you write a word, you draw the letters first and finish with one continuous stroke across the top:

**कमल** (kamal) — क, म, ल joined by one unbroken headline.

Practical consequences for a learner:

- **Words are visual blocks.** The unbroken headline is how your eye learns to spot where one word ends and the next begins, since the letters inside merge into a single hanging unit.
- **Some letters break the line.** A few characters, like ध (dha) and भ (bha), have a small gap or loop at the top; that's normal, not sloppy writing.
- **Mātrās can sit above the line.** The signs for **i** (ि), **e** (े), **ai** (ै), **o** (ो), **au** (ौ) live partly or wholly above the headline — कि (ki) is famous: its mātrā is written *before* the consonant but pronounced *after* it.

Don't fight the headline. Writing it last, in one stroke, is exactly how Hindi schoolchildren are taught, and it makes handwriting faster, not slower.
Give me the full Devanagari consonant chart with transliteration so I can learn the system.

The 33 core consonants, arranged the way Indian grammarians organized them over two thousand years ago — by where in the mouth each sound is made, throat to lips. Read down the first five rows: voiceless, voiceless-aspirated, voiced, voiced-aspirated, nasal.

| group | plain | aspirated | voiced | voiced + asp. | nasal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| velar (throat) | क ka | ख kha | ग ga | घ gha | ङ ṅa |
| palatal (palate) | च ca | छ cha | ज ja | झ jha | ञ ña |
| retroflex (tongue curled back) | ट ṭa | ठ ṭha | ड ḍa | ढ ḍha | ण ṇa |
| dental (teeth) | त ta | थ tha | द da | ध dha | न na |
| labial (lips) | प pa | फ pha | ब ba | भ bha | म ma |

Then the liquids and glides: य **ya**, र **ra**, ल **la**, व **va**.

Then the sibilants and h: श **śa**, ष **ṣa**, स **sa**, ह **ha**.

And the independent vowels: अ **a**, आ **ā**, इ **i**, ई **ī**, उ **u**, ऊ **ū**, ऋ **ṛ**, ए **e**, ऐ **ai**, ओ **o**, औ **au**.

Two things to notice. First, the grid is a map of your mouth — each row moves one step forward. Second, ङ (ṅa) and ञ (ña) are rare as standalone letters; you mostly meet them as the dot ं before a consonant, as in हिंदी (hindī) itself.
How do the vowel signs (matras) actually work? Show me with one consonant.

Take क (ka) and dress it in every vowel. The independent vowel letter is used at the start of a word; the mātrā (sign) is used when the vowel follows a consonant:

| vowel | alone | sign with क | read |
|---|---|---|---|
| a | अ | क | ka |
| ā | आ | का | kā |
| i | इ | कि | ki |
| ī | ई | की | kī |
| u | उ | कु | ku |
| ū | ऊ | कू | kū |
| e | ए | के | ke |
| ai | ऐ | कै | kai |
| o | ओ | को | ko |
| au | औ | कौ | kau |

Real words built this way: **काम** (kām, work), **किताब** (kitāb, book), **कुर्सी** (kursī, chair), **केला** (kelā, banana), **कौन** (kaun, who).

Three placement quirks, all regular:

- **ि (i) is written on the left** of the consonant but read after it: कि is *ki*, never *ik*.
- **ु and ू tuck underneath**: कु, कू. With र they fuse specially: रु (ru), रू (rū).
- **े ै ो ौ ride on top**, above the headline: के, कै, को, कौ.

Learn this one table and you can sound out any Hindi word ever written — slowly at first, but with zero guessing.
What is the halant, and why does नमस्ते need it?

The **halant** (हलन्त), also called **virām**, is the small diagonal slash under a consonant that cancels its built-in "a": क् is pure **k**, no vowel. It matters because Hindi loves consonant clusters, and a cluster means the first consonant must lose its vowel.

**नमस्ते** (namaste) is the perfect first example. Break it down:

न **na** + म **ma** + स् **s** (halant — no vowel!) + ते **te** = **namaste**

Without the halant, स would be read "sa" and the word would come out *namasate*. The स् + त combination also fuses visually into the conjunct **स्त** (sta) — that stacked shape in the middle of नमस्ते is one of the most common conjuncts in the language.

More clusters you'll meet in week one:

- **क्या** (kyā, what) — क् + य = क्य
- **अच्छा** (acchā, good) — च् + छ = च्छ
- **स्कूल** (skūl, school) — स् + क = स्क

In handwriting and print, the halant sometimes shows as the visible slash (क्) and sometimes disappears into a fused conjunct shape (स्त). Recognizing both forms is the whole skill.
I keep seeing strange fused letters like क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ. What are they?

Those are **conjunct consonants** (संयुक्ताक्षर) — two or three consonants fused into one glyph when no vowel separates them. Three are so common they were historically taught as letters in their own right:

- **क्ष (kṣa)** = क् + ष. You meet it in **क्षमा** (kṣamā, forgiveness), **शिक्षा** (śikṣā, education), **कक्षा** (kakṣā, class/classroom).
- **त्र (tra)** = त् + र. In **मित्र** (mitra, friend), **पत्र** (patra, letter), **त्रिभुज** (tribhuj, triangle).
- **ज्ञ (jña)** = ज् + ञ. In **ज्ञान** (jñān, knowledge). Honest pronunciation note: in everyday Hindi this is spoken **"gyān"** — almost nobody says a careful "jña." The spelling preserves Sanskrit; the tongue follows Hindi.

Beyond the famous three, conjuncts follow patterns you can decode rather than memorize:

- र underneath becomes a small hook or slash: **क्रम** (kram, order/sequence).
- र on top of a following consonant becomes a little arc (reph) written over the *next* letter: **कर्म** (karma) is written क + र् + म but the arc sits above म.
- Doubled consonants stack: **बुद्ध** (buddh) in बुद्ध (Buddha), द् + ध.

Strategy: learn क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ by sight, learn the र rules, and decode the rest on the fly. That's genuinely all native readers do.
Can you walk me through reading an actual shop sign, letter by letter?

Here's a sign you'll see on thousands of Indian streets:

**शुद्ध शाकाहारी भोजनालय**
śuddh śākāhārī bhojanālaya — "Pure Vegetarian Eatery"

**शुद्ध (śuddh, pure)** — शु = श (śa) with the u-mātrā tucked below: **śu**. Then द्ध — a conjunct, द् + ध stacked: **ddh**. (The doubled sound is why it's transliterated with two d's.)

**शाकाहारी (śākāhārī, vegetarian)** — शा **śā** (long ā stroke on the right), का **kā**, हा **hā**, री **rī** (long ī curling over the top). Notice the pattern: this word is a treadmill of long ā's — śā-kā-hā-rī. It's built from शाक (śāk, vegetables/greens) + आहारी (āhārī, one who eats...), so literally "vegetable-eater."

**भोजनालय (bhojanālaya, eatery)** — भो **bho** (o-mātrā on top), ज **ja**, ना **nā**, ल **la**, य **ya**. भोजन (bhojan) is the formal word for a meal, and आलय (ālaya) means "house/abode" — same ālaya as in हिमालय (Himālaya, "abode of snow"). A "meal-house."

Why this sign is worth your time: **शुद्ध शाकाहारी** on a restaurant is a cultural promise, not just a menu note — it signals food cooked without meat, egg, and often without onion and garlic. Reading the sign tells you how to behave inside it.
Can I just learn Hindi in Roman letters and skip the script?

You can get surprisingly far, and then you hit a wall that transliteration itself built. Here's the honest accounting.

**What Roman letters can't show you:**

- **Two different t's.** ताल (tāl, rhythm) uses a *dental* त; टाल (ṭāl, postpone) uses a *retroflex* ट. In casual Roman spelling both become "taal" — but they're different words, and a Hindi ear hears them as clearly as you hear "pat" vs "bat."
- **Aspiration.** काल (kāl, time) vs खाल (khāl, skin) differ only in a puff of air. Texting Hindi in Roman letters drops this constantly, and native readers reconstruct it from context. You, the learner, can't yet.
- **Vowel length.** दिन (din, day) vs दीन (dīn, humble/poor). Roman "din" for both hides a meaning-bearing difference.

**What the script gives you for free:** perfect spelling-to-sound mapping, access to signs, menus, messages, and subtitles as they're actually written, and pronunciation that natives rate as noticeably better.

**The working compromise:** learn with both for the first month — Devanagari on top, transliteration beneath, like the records in this course do. Then drop the Roman line for words you know. Most learners find the script stops being scary around week three; the alphabet-sized effort buys a lifetime skill. Skipping it entirely is the one shortcut that reliably becomes a ceiling.
What do the dots mean — the dot above (ं), the moon-dot (ँ), and the dot below in ज़?

Three different dots, three different jobs. Don't merge them.

**1. Anusvār (ं) — the plain dot above.** It stands for a nasal sound that borrows its flavor from the next consonant: before क it sounds like "ng," before त like "n." So **हिंदी** (hindī) and **रंग** (raṅg, color) both wear it. In **संगीत** (saṅgīt, music) it makes the "ng" in "sangeet."

**2. Candrabindu (ँ) — the moon-and-dot.** This one nasalizes the *vowel itself*: the sound resonates through the nose. **माँ** (māṅ, mother), **चाँद** (cāṅd, moon), **गाँव** (gāṅv, village), **हँसी** (haṅsī, laughter). The contrast is real: **हंस** (haṅs) is a swan; **हँस** (haṅs, with candrabindu) is "laugh!" Same letters, different dot, different word.

**3. Nuktā (़) — the dot below.** It creates sounds Hindi borrowed from Persian, Arabic, and English: क़ **qa**, ख़ **kha (deep kh)**, ग़ **ġa**, ज़ **za**, फ़ **fa**, plus the flaps ड़ **ṛa** and ढ़ **ṛha**. So **ज़िंदगी** (zindagī, life), **ख़बर** (khabar, news), **फ़िल्म** (film). In casual print the nuktā is often dropped — you'll see जिंदगी written without dots — but in careful writing it's standard, and it changes meaning: **राज** (rāj, rule/kingdom) vs **राज़** (rāz, secret).
दुकान के बोर्ड पर लिखा है — "ताज़ा फल और सब्ज़ी"। इसका क्या मतलब है?

बहुत अच्छा सवाल! आइए इसे धीरे-धीरे पढ़ें।

**ताज़ा (tāzā)** — मतलब: fresh, नया और ताज़ा। यह शब्द फ़ारसी से आया है। देखें, ज़ के नीचे बिंदु (नुक्ता) है — इसलिए आवाज़ "za" है।
*Tāzā matlab: fresh.*

**फल (phal)** — मतलब: fruit। ध्यान दें — फ की आवाज़ "pha" है, "fa" नहीं। फ़ (नुक्ते वाला) होता तो "fa" होता।
*Phal matlab: fruit.*

**और (aur)** — मतलब: and। यह छोटा शब्द हर वाक्य में मिलता है।
*Aur matlab: and.*

**सब्ज़ी (sabzī)** — मतलब: vegetable। इसमें भी ज़ है, इसलिए "sabzī" पढ़ें।
*Sabzī matlab: vegetable.*

तो पूरे बोर्ड का मतलब है: **"Fresh fruit and vegetables."**

एक छोटी बात: दुकान के बोर्ड पर अक्सर ऐसे ही छोटे और साफ़ शब्द होते हैं। अगर आप "ताज़ा", "शुद्ध", "सस्ता" (sastā, cheap) और "ख़ास" (khās, special) पहचान लें, तो आधे बोर्ड आप ख़ुद पढ़ लेंगे।
*(Ek choṭī bāt: dukān ke borḍ par aksar aise hī choṭe aur sāf śabd hote haiṅ. Agar āp ye śabd pahcān leṅ, to ādhe borḍ āp khud paṛh leṅge.)*
My teacher keeps correcting my "t" sounds. Hindi has TWO t's?

Two t's, two d's — and the difference is where your tongue lands.

**Dental त (ta) / द (da):** the tongue tip touches the *back of your upper teeth* — literally dental. English speakers don't have this stop; the closest feel is the soft t in Spanish or French. It's light and forward.

**Retroflex ट (ṭa) / ड (ḍa):** curl the tongue tip *back* so it taps the hard palate behind the ridge, then release. This is actually close to how Americans say "t" and "d" in "top" and "dog" — your native t is nearer the retroflex than the dental.

Minimal pairs where the tongue position alone changes the word:

- **ताल (tāl)** — rhythm; also a lake/pond — vs **टाल (ṭāl)** — postpone, put off
- **दाल (dāl)** — lentils — vs **डाल (ḍāl)** — a branch; also "put/pour!"
- **तीन (tīn)** — three (dental) — vs **टीन (ṭīn)** — tin metal

Practice trick: say "tea" while pressing your tongue tip firmly against your teeth — that's त. Then curl back and flick for ट. Hindi ears treat these as different consonants entirely, the way you treat "d" and "g" as different. Nobody will misunderstand you catastrophically with the wrong one, but the right one is what makes natives say your Hindi "sounds clean."
What does "aspirated" mean, and can a puff of air really change a word's meaning?

Aspiration is a small burst of air that follows the consonant — hold your palm before your lips and say English "pin" (big puff) versus "spin" (almost none). Hindi weaponizes that difference: for every plain stop there is a separate aspirated letter, and the puff alone can change the word.

- **काल (kāl)** — time, era — vs **खाल (khāl)** — skin, hide
- **पल (pal)** — a moment — vs **फल (phal)** — fruit
- **दान (dān)** — a donation — vs **धान (dhān)** — paddy, unhusked rice
- **कान (kān)** — ear — vs **खान (khān)** — a mine

So खाना (khānā, food / to eat) begins with the aspirated kh — if you say kānā you're saying something closer to "one-eyed," a classic learner stumble that Hindi speakers find genuinely funny.

The good news: aspiration is mechanical, not subtle. Practice by holding a tissue in front of your mouth: क should barely move it, ख should make it jump. Your mouth already owns this skill from English "pin/spin" — Hindi just asks you to deploy it on purpose, in every position, including the middle of words: पढ़ना (paṛhnā, to read/study) has its aspiration right in the center.
Is there a logic to how Hindi consonants are organized, or do I just memorize them?

There's a logic so good that linguists consider the Indian arrangement one of the great intellectual achievements of the ancient world. The 25 main stops form a **5 × 5 grid indexed by your mouth**.

Move down the rows and the contact point walks forward, throat to lips: **velar** (क row, at the soft palate) → **palatal** (च row) → **retroflex** (ट row, tongue curled back) → **dental** (त row, tongue on teeth) → **labial** (प row, lips).

Move across any row and the *manner* changes in a fixed sequence: voiceless (क ka) → voiceless aspirated (ख kha) → voiced (ग ga) → voiced aspirated (घ gha) → nasal (ङ ṅa).

So if someone gives you the coordinates "dental, voiced, aspirated," there is exactly one letter that can be: **ध (dha)**. The chart isn't a list to memorize; it's a machine that generates the sounds.

Why this matters practically: when a teacher says "that's the aspirated partner," or a dictionary orders words (Hindi dictionaries follow this exact grid, not a-b-c), or you need the nasal that matches a consonant — the grid answers. Two thousand years before the IPA chart, Paninian grammarians had already built one. Learn the grid once and the alphabet stops being 33 strangers.
How do I pronounce the nasalized vowels, like in माँ (mother) and चाँद (moon)?

Nasalization means part of the air escapes through your nose *while* you say the vowel — the vowel itself hums. English does this faintly before n and m ("sing," "home"); Hindi makes it a full, meaning-carrying feature, written with the candrabindu (ँ).

- **माँ (māṅ)** — mother
- **चाँद (cāṅd)** — moon
- **गाँव (gāṅv)** — village
- **आँख (āṅkh)** — eye
- **हँसी (haṅsī)** — laughter

Technique: say a long "āāā" and, mid-sound, let the back of your tongue relax so air diverts up into the nose. You'll feel a buzz behind your nose. French speakers: it's the same gesture as in "bon" or "vent," just on long vowels.

Where learners go wrong: turning it into a full "n" or "ng" consonant — saying "māng" for माँ. Keep it a *flavor* of the vowel, not an extra letter. And note the stakes: **माँग (māṅg, a demand/parting of hair)** with a full anusvār is a different word from **माँ (māṅ)**. Context rescues you almost always, but the clean version costs little to learn: hum the vowel, don't add a consonant.
Why is नमक pronounced "namak" and not "namaka"? The last letter looks like it should have a vowel.

You've found **schwa deletion** — the single biggest gap between Hindi spelling and Hindi speech. The inherent "a" written into every consonant is often *not pronounced*, by rules that are tendencies, not iron laws.

**Rule one — the final schwa is always silent.** A word-final consonant never sounds its "a" in standard Hindi:

- राम = **Rām**, not "Rāma" (in Hindi; Sanskrit and some other Indian languages differ)
- किताब = **kitāb**, not "kitāba"
- नमक = **namak**, not "namaka"

**Rule two — middle schwas often drop too,** roughly when a full vowel follows in the next syllable: कमल = **kamal** (not "kamala"), समझ = **samajh** (understanding), आदमी = **ādmī**. The rhythm tends toward deleting every second light "a" — but this one is a tendency with real exceptions, and dropping the wrong one is a classic learner error. लड़की stays **laṛkī** — never "laṛakī" (the spelling-pronunciation, with every written vowel sounded). Which middle schwas drop and which survive is only partly predictable: the first syllable's schwa never drops, deletions favor light middle syllables, and even then there are famous exceptions — लड़की keeping its vowel is one.

**The safe method:** never trust the spelling alone for rhythm. Learn each word as a *sound* with the spelling as its portrait — which is why this course always pairs Devanagari with transliteration. Long vowels (ā, ī, ū) and mātrā vowels are never deleted; only the little inherent "a" plays this disappearing trick.
What are the flapping sounds in लड़का and पढ़ाई? English doesn't have them.

Those are the **retroflex flaps** ड़ (ṛa) and ढ़ (ṛha) — written as ड and ढ with a nuktā dot below. The tongue curls back and *flicks* once against the palate, a single tap, rather than holding a stop.

The surprise: you already make this sound. The middle of American "butter," "ladder," or "city" is nearly the same flick — Hindi just uses it as a full consonant that can start syllables anywhere in a word.

- **लड़का (laṛkā)** — boy
- **लड़की (laṛkī)** — girl
- **पढ़ाई (paṛhāī)** — studies
- **बड़ा (baṛā)** — big
- **घोड़ा (ghoṛā)** — horse

Pattern worth knowing: ड and ढ often *soften* into ड़ and ढ़ between vowels — बड़ा is historically the same word-family as its spelling suggests. And the flap never starts a native word, which is a free pronunciation check: if you see ड़ at the start, it's a loanword or a name.

Practice by saying "ladder" the American way, then isolating that middle flick: la-ṛ-kā. Two minutes of that and लड़का stops sounding like "ludka" — the error every beginner makes, and every Hindi speaker gently hears.
Does vowel length really matter, or will people understand me anyway?

It matters the way it matters in English "ship/sheep" — context saves you often, but the language treats short and long as different sounds, and minimal pairs are everywhere:

- **दिन (din)** — day — vs **दीन (dīn)** — humble, poor
- **कल (kal)** — tomorrow/yesterday — vs **काल (kāl)** — time, an era
- **मिल (mil)** — meet! / a mill — vs **मील (mīl)** — a mile
- **कुल (kul)** — total; family line — vs **कूल (kūl)** — a riverbank (formal)

The practical rule: a long vowel is held roughly *twice* as long — it's a timing difference, not a tone or pitch difference. English speakers tend to shorten Hindi long vowels and lengthen short ones under stress, which is the single most audible foreign accent in Hindi.

Two anchors that will carry you far:

- **पानी (pānī, water)** — hear both long vowels held: pā-nī.
- **किताब (kitāb, book)** — the ā is long, the i is short: ki-tāb, quick-then-held.

And a mercy: Hindi spelling shows length perfectly (ि vs ी, ु vs ू, अ vs आ). Unlike English, if you can read it, you know exactly how long to hold it.
ताल और टाल में क्या फ़र्क है? दोनों "taal" ही सुनाई देते हैं।

बहुत अच्छा सवाल — यह हिंदी की सबसे ज़रूरी आवाज़ों में से एक है।

**ताल (tāl)** — इसमें त **दाँतों** से बोलते हैं। जीभ की नोक ऊपर के दाँतों को छूती है। ताल का मतलब है: rhythm, या एक छोटी झील।
*(Tāl meṅ ta dāntoṅ se bolte haiṅ — jībh kī nok dāntoṅ ko chūtī hai.)*

**टाल (ṭāl)** — इसमें ट बोलते समय जीभ **पीछे मुड़ती** है और तालु (मुँह की छत) को छूती है। टाल का मतलब है: postpone, टालना।
*(Ṭāl meṅ jībh pīche muṛtī hai aur tālu ko chūtī hai.)*

दोनों का अभ्यास करें:
- **ताल** — ताल (rhythm) — जीभ दाँतों पर
- **टाल** — टाल (postpone) — जीभ पीछे

एक और जोड़ी सुनें:
- **दाल (dāl)** — खाने वाली दाल (lentils)
- **डाल (ḍāl)** — पेड़ की डाल (branch)

अंग्रेज़ी बोलने वालों के लिए ख़ुशख़बरी: आपकी "t" और "d" की आवाज़ असल में ट और ड के ज़्यादा करीब है। तो टाल आपके लिए आसान है — बस ताल के लिए जीभ को दाँतों तक लाना सीखना है।
*(Aṅgrezī bolne vāloṅ ke liye khuśkhabrī: āpkī "t" kī āvāz ṭa ke zyādā qarīb hai. Bas tāl ke liye jībh ko dāntoṅ tak lānā sīkhnā hai.)*
Hindi seems to have three "s" sounds — श, ष, स. Do I really need all three?

Honest answer: you need two actively and one passively, and here's the real distribution.

- **स (sa)** — the plain s of English "sun." The workhorse: **सब** (sab, all), **साल** (sāl, year).
- **श (śa)** — the "sh" of English "ship." Equally common: **शहर** (śahar, city), **शुक्रिया** (śukriyā, thank you), **शांति** (śānti, peace).
- **ष (ṣa)** — a retroflex sh, tongue curled back. It survives mostly inside Sanskrit-derived words and conjuncts: **विषय** (viṣay, subject/topic), **कृष्ण** (Kṛṣṇa), and the conjunct क्ष (kṣa). In everyday speech across much of the Hindi belt, ष is pronounced the same as श — even many native speakers merge them outside formal registers.

So the working rule: keep स and श clearly apart (साल sāl "year" vs शाल śāl "a shawl" is a real pair), and learn to *recognize* ष in writing without agonizing over producing a distinct third sound. Your spelling, though, must respect it — विषय written with the wrong sibilant looks as wrong to a Hindi reader as "seperate" does to you.

One more member of the family, borrowed and proud: **ज़ (za)** with the nuktā — ज़रूर (zarūr, certainly), ज़िंदगी (zindagī, life). That one you must produce distinctly; merging it into ज (ja) changes words.
Where does the stress fall in Hindi words? I don't want to sound like I'm singing English at it.

Hindi stress is gentle, and the good news is that getting it "wrong" almost never blocks meaning — Hindi is not a stress-contrastive language the way English is (think REcord vs reCORD). But rhythm is a big part of sounding natural, and Hindi rhythm follows **weight**, not fixed positions.

The working principles:

- **Heavy syllables attract stress.** A syllable is heavy if it has a long vowel or ends in a consonant: कि**ताब** (ki-**tāb**, book), **बा**ज़ार (bā-zār, market) leans on its long vowels; in बाज़ार the final heavy syllable carries the most weight.
- **Speech is syllable-timed.** English crushes unstressed syllables into schwas ("banana" → b'nana). Hindi gives each syllable roughly its full value: **केला** is ke-lā, two clean beats, never "k'la."
- **Don't import English question melody wholesale.** Hindi yes/no questions often just add क्या (kyā) at the front rather than relying on a rising tune.

The one real trap is *reducing* vowels. If you keep every vowel at full value, hold long vowels long, and let heavy syllables land a little firmer, your rhythm will read as Hindi even while your accent is still forming. Hindi listeners forgive consonant slips far more readily than English-style vowel-swallowing.
How does Hindi sentence order work? Where does the verb go?

Hindi is an **SOV** language: Subject – Object – Verb, with the verb anchored at the end. English says "I read a book"; Hindi arranges the same words as "I book read":

**मैं किताब पढ़ता हूँ।**
Maiṅ kitāb paṛhtā hūṅ. — "I read a book." (lit. I book read am)

**वह चाय पीती है।**
Vo cāy pītī hai. — "She drinks tea." (lit. She tea drinks is)

Two consequences to internalize early:

1. **The verb carries the information payload** — tense, gender, number, respect — and it arrives last. Hindi listeners wait for the end of your sentence the way English listeners wait for the verb in the middle. Don't panic if you can't tell what a long sentence is *doing* until it lands; that's normal Hindi processing, even for natives.

2. **Modifiers cluster before what they modify**, including entire phrases: "the book *that is on the table*" stacks up before "book." English's right-branching ("the book on the table in the room...") flips to left-branching.

The practical comfort: word order inside the sentence is more flexible than English for emphasis (see how phrases move for focus), but that verb-final anchor barely ever moves. Build every sentence by placing the verb last and you have the skeleton right.
What are postpositions? I've only ever used prepositions.

A postposition is a preposition that shows up *after* its noun instead of before. English puts the relation first ("in the room," "to Delhi"); Hindi puts the noun first and tags the relation onto its back:

- **कमरे में** (kamre **meṅ**) — in the room
- **दिल्ली को** (Dillī **ko**) — to Delhi
- **मेज़ पर** (mez **par**) — on the table
- **दोस्त से** (dost **se**) — from/with/by a friend

The big five to learn first:

| postposition | core job | example |
|---|---|---|
| में (meṅ) | in, inside | घर में (ghar meṅ, in the house) |
| पर (par) | on, at | मेज़ पर (mez par, on the table) |
| को (ko) | to, for; marks specific objects | मुझे (mujhe, to me) |
| से (se) | from, with, by, than | दिल्ली से (Dillī se, from Delhi) |
| का/के/की (kā/ke/kī) | of, 's (possession) | राम का घर (Rām kā ghar, Ram's house) |

One mechanical wrinkle you'll meet immediately: a noun changes shape before a postposition (its **oblique** form) — कमरा (kamrā, room) becomes कमरे में (kamre meṅ). And pronouns fuse with को: मैं + को = मुझे (mujhe). Treat those fused pronoun forms as vocabulary items and the system feels much smaller than it looks.
Give me a reference table of the main Hindi postpositions and what each one does.

The core postpositions. Hindi stacks the relation after the noun; the noun (if it can change) appears in its oblique form before them.

| postposition | transliteration | core meanings | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| का / के / की | kā / ke / kī | of, 's — agrees with the thing possessed | राम की किताब (Rām kī kitāb, Ram's book) |
| को | ko | to, for; marks a specific/definite object | बच्चे को (bacce ko, to the child) |
| से | se | from; with (instrument); by; than (in comparisons) | चाकू से (cākū se, with a knife) |
| में | meṅ | in, inside, among | शहर में (śahar meṅ, in the city) |
| पर | par | on, at, upon | दीवार पर (dīvār par, on the wall) |
| तक | tak | up to, until, as far as | सोमवार तक (somvār tak, until Monday) |
| के लिए | ke liye | for (the benefit of) | बच्चों के लिए (baccoṅ ke liye, for the children) |
| के बाद | ke bād | after | खाने के बाद (khāne ke bād, after eating) |
| के पास | ke pās | near; in someone's possession | स्टेशन के पास (sṭeśan ke pās, near the station) |
| के सामने | ke sāmne | in front of, opposite | घर के सामने (ghar ke sāmne, in front of the house) |
| के साथ | ke sāth | together with | दोस्तों के साथ (dostoṅ ke sāth, with friends) |
| के बिना | ke binā | without | चीनी के बिना (cīnī ke binā, without sugar) |

Note the two-part ones: के लिए, के बाद and friends are built on the genitive के plus a noun — which is why they need the oblique के even before feminine nouns. राम के लिए (Rām ke liye, for Ram) never becomes *की लिए. The के in these compounds is frozen.
The verb ending changes when a woman does something? Show me how.

Yes — Hindi verbs agree with their subject in **gender and number**, and the ending is where you see it. In the present habitual, the pattern is a clean three-way split:

- **लड़का पढ़ता है।** (Laṛkā paṛhtā hai.) — The boy reads/studies. (masc. sg. **-tā**)
- **लड़की पढ़ती है।** (Laṛkī paṛhtī hai.) — The girl reads. (fem. sg. **-tī**)
- **लड़के पढ़ते हैं।** (Laṛke paṛhte haiṅ.) — The boys read. (pl. **-te**)
- **लड़कियाँ पढ़ती हैं।** (Laṛkiyāṅ paṛhtī haiṅ.) — The girls read. (fem. pl. keeps **-tī**, verb हैं)

The same -ā / -ī / -e melody runs through the whole language: अच्छा/अच्छी/अच्छे (good), गया/गई/गए (went), बड़ा/बड़ी/बड़े (big). Once your ear owns that tune, you can often predict an ending you've never formally learned.

Two comforts. First, the feminine plural usually matches the feminine singular in the participle (पढ़ती) — only the auxiliary हैं changes. Second, **आप** and respected elders take plural forms even for one person: **माताजी पढ़ती हैं** (Mātājī paṛhtī haiṅ) — "Mother reads," with the plural auxiliary as a mark of respect.

And the trap to unlearn early: English speakers want to say *वह पढ़ता है about a woman because English verbs don't care. Hindi verbs always care.
Why does "Ram's" come out three ways — का, के, की?

Because का isn't really "of" — it's an adjective in disguise, and it agrees with the **thing possessed**, not with the possessor. Watch the same owner with three different possessions:

- **राम का घर** (Rām **kā** ghar) — Ram's house. घर (ghar, house) is masculine singular → **kā**
- **राम की किताब** (Rām **kī** kitāb) — Ram's book. किताब (kitāb, book) is feminine → **kī**
- **राम के दोस्त** (Rām **ke** dost) — Ram's friends. Plural → **ke**
- **राम के घर में** (Rām **ke** ghar meṅ) — in Ram's house. घर before a postposition (oblique) → **ke**

The rule, complete in one line: **kā** for masculine singular direct, **kī** for feminine (any number), **ke** for masculine plural *and* whenever the possessed noun stands before another postposition.

This is the same -ā/-ī/-e melody as adjectives (अच्छा/अच्छी/अच्छे), because grammatically का behaves exactly like one. Once you stop translating it as the word "of" and start treating it as a linker that dresses to match its noun, the three forms stop being a memorization task and become automatic.

Quick self-check set: मेरी माँ (merī māṅ, my mother — fem.), मेरा भाई (merā bhāī, my brother — masc.), मेरे भाई के साथ (mere bhāī ke sāth, with my brother — oblique, so के after भाई and मेरे before it).
Where do question words go in Hindi? Do they move to the front like in English?

No — and this is a gift. Hindi question words **stay where the answer would go** (in situ). English scrambles "You are going *where*?" into "*Where* are you going?"; Hindi leaves the word in place:

- **तुम कहाँ जा रहे हो?** (Tum **kahāṅ** jā rahe ho?) — Where are you going? (कहाँ sits in the middle, where the place-answer would sit.)
- **यह कितने का है?** (Yah **kitne** kā hai?) — How much is this?
- **तुमने किसको बुलाया?** (Tumne **kisko** bulāyā?) — Whom did you call? (किसको = who + को, in object position.)
- **वह क्यों नहीं आया?** (Vo **kyoṅ** nahīṅ āyā?) — Why didn't he come?

The question words themselves: क्या (kyā, what), कौन (kaun, who), कहाँ (kahāṅ, where), कब (kab, when), क्यों (kyoṅ, why), कैसा (kaisā, how/what kind), कितना (kitnā, how much/many) — कैसा and कितना agree in gender like adjectives: कितने का (for masc.), कितनी (fem.).

Yes/no questions work differently: either put **क्या** at the very front — **क्या तुम आ रहे हो?** (Kyā tum ā rahe ho? Are you coming?) — or simply use rising intonation: **तुम आ रहे हो?** Same words, question tune. Notice there are two different क्या jobs: front-of-sentence क्या means "is it the case that...?", while क्या in object position means "what?" — **तुम क्या खा रहे हो?** (Tum kyā khā rahe ho? What are you eating?)
Do Hindi speakers really drop the subject all the time? How do you know who's doing what?

Constantly — and the verb tells you. Hindi verbs encode person and gender in their endings, so the subject is often recoverable from the verb alone, and conversation drops it whenever context has already established it.

- — **समझ गया।** (Samajh gayā.) — "(I) understood." गया's masculine -ā ending plus context points to the speaker; a woman says **समझ गई** (samajh gaī) and the ending still identifies her.
- — **आ रहे हो?** (Ā rahe ho?) — "(Are you) coming?" The हो ending can *only* belong to तुम — no other subject fits.
- — **खाना खाया?** (Khānā khāyā?) — "(Did you) eat?" Pure context at work.

Compare English, where dropping the subject sounds like a telegram or a diary ("Went to store. Bought milk."). In Hindi it's the unmarked conversational style; keeping मैं in every sentence sounds stiff and oddly self-focused, like saying "I" with italics all day.

Two safety rails for learners. First, drop subjects only when the reference is genuinely obvious — when two men are in play, *वह गया* (vo gayā) needs names. Second, the pronoun **वह/वो** itself is dropped less casually than मैं/तुम, because third persons are the ones context loses track of. Speak like a native: establish the cast, then let the endings do the work.
If Hindi word order is flexible, how do I know what a sentence emphasizes?

Hindi's flexibility is real but not random — the neutral order is Subject–Object–Verb, and **moving a phrase is how you spotlight it**. The phrase that lands **right before the verb** gets the focus, and fronting something to the start makes it the topic. Compare three versions of "Ram gave the book to Sita":

- **राम ने सीता को किताब दी।** (Rām ne Sītā ko kitāb dī.) — Neutral report. किताब before the verb gets mild focus: the *book* is what he gave.
- **राम ने किताब सीता को दी।** (Rām ne kitāb Sītā ko dī.) — सीता को sits before दी: focus on *Sita* — she's the one he gave it to (not someone else).
- **किताब राम ने सीता को दी।** (Kitāb Rām ne Sītā ko dī.) — किताब fronted as topic: "As for the book — Ram gave it to Sita." You're now talking *about the book's* fate.

What barely ever moves: the **verb stays final**, and postpositions stay glued to their nouns (you move किताब को as a block, never *को किताब). Particles and negation also cluster near the verb: नहीं usually stands immediately before it.

So read scrambled Hindi by asking two questions: what was fronted (that's the topic), and what's sitting just before the verb (that's the point). English does this job with stress and "it was X who..." constructions; Hindi does it with position. It's a different instrument playing the same music.
हिंदी में क्रिया हमेशा वाक्य के अंत में क्यों आती है?

अच्छा प्रश्न! सीधा उत्तर है — हिंदी की बनावट ही ऐसी है। हिंदी **SOV** भाषा है: पहले कर्ता (subject), फिर कर्म (object), और अंत में क्रिया (verb)।

देखें:
- **मैं चाय पीता हूँ।** (Maiṅ cāy pītā hūṅ.) — I drink tea.
- **वह एक किताब पढ़ रही है।** (Vo ek kitāb paṛh rahī hai.) — She is reading a book.

अंग्रेज़ी में कहते हैं "I drink tea" — क्रिया बीच में। हिंदी में क्रिया अंत तक रुकती है, इसलिए सुनने वाला पूरे वाक्य का इंतज़ार करता है।

एक मज़ेदार बात: क्योंकि क्रिया अंत में आती है, क्रिया से **ठीक पहले** वाला शब्द सबसे ज़्यादा ज़ोर (focus) पाता है।

- **राम ने मुझे किताब दी।** (Rām ne mujhe kitāb dī.) — ज़ोर "किताब" पर है।
- **राम ने किताब मुझे दी।** (Rām ne kitāb mujhe dī.) — अब ज़ोर "मुझे" पर है।

तो नियम याद रखें: **क्रिया अंत में, और ज़ोर क्रिया से पहले।**
*(To niyam yād rakheṅ: kriyā ant meṅ, aur zor kriyā se pahle.)*
How does Hindi say "not", "don't", and "never"?

Three negators, three different jobs — and using the wrong one is a classic beginner tell.

**नहीं (nahīṅ)** — the ordinary "not," standing just before the verb:

- **मैं नहीं जा रहा।** (Maiṅ nahīṅ jā rahā.) — I'm not going.
- **वह हिंदी नहीं बोलती।** (Vo hindī nahīṅ boltī.) — She doesn't speak Hindi.

Quirk: with habitual verbs, नहीं often *absorbs* the auxiliary — **मैं चाय नहीं पीता** (maiṅ cāy nahīṅ pītā) drops the हूँ and sounds perfectly natural, even preferred in casual speech.

**मत (mat)** — "don't!" for commands and prohibitions only:

- **मत जाओ!** (Mat jāo!) — Don't go!
- **शोर मत करो।** (Śor mat karo.) — Don't make noise.

**न (na)** — the soft, polite "please don't / let's not" of requests and suggestions:

- **न जाएँ तो अच्छा हो।** (Na jāeṅ to acchā ho.) — It'd be better if we didn't go. (subjunctive flavor)
- In tags it also means "right?/isn't it?": **तुम आ रहे हो, न?** (Tum ā rahe ho, na? — You're coming, right?)

And "never" is कभी नहीं (kabhī nahīṅ) — **मैं कभी वहाँ नहीं गया** (maiṅ kabhī vahāṅ nahīṅ gayā, I've never been there). Word order in one line: नहीं hugs the verb, मत replaces नहीं in commands, and न is for gentle, hypothetical, or tag-question territory.
Teach me होना (to be). I gather everything hangs off it.

होना (honā) is the spine of Hindi — present tense first, because you'll use it in nearly every sentence:

| person | form | example |
|---|---|---|
| मैं (I) | **हूँ** (hūṅ) | मैं ठीक हूँ। (Maiṅ ṭhīk hūṅ. I'm fine.) |
| तू (you, intimate) | **है** (hai) | तू कैसा है? (Tū kaisā hai?) |
| तुम (you) | **हो** (ho) | तुम कहाँ हो? (Tum kahāṅ ho? Where are you?) |
| आप (you, respectful) | **हैं** (haiṅ) | आप कैसे हैं? (Āp kaise haiṅ?) |
| यह/वह (he/she/this/that) | **है** (hai) | वह मेरा दोस्त है। (Vo merā dost hai.) |
| हम/वे (we/they) | **हैं** (haiṅ) | वे घर पर हैं। (Ve ghar par haiṅ.) |

The past tense agrees in **gender and number** instead of person:

- masc. sg. **था** (thā) — वह बीमार था। (Vo bīmār thā. He was ill.)
- fem. sg. **थी** (thī) — वह बीमार थी। (She was ill.)
- masc. pl. / respect **थे** (the) — वे वहाँ थे। (They were there.)
- fem. pl. / respect **थीं** (thīṅ) — वे वहाँ थीं। (They — women — were there.)

Why it matters beyond "to be": these same forms ride as auxiliaries in almost every tense — पढ़ता **है** (reads), पढ़ रहा **था** (was reading), गया **है** (has gone). Master होना and you've pre-learned the tail of half the verb system. The future (होगा hogā, fem. होगी hogī, pl. होंगे hoṅge) appears in predictions: **कल बारिश होगी** (Kal bāriś hogī — It will rain tomorrow; बारिश is feminine, hence होगी).
How do I say what someone habitually does — "she teaches," "I get up early"?

The **habitual present**: verb stem + **-tā / -tī / -te** + होना in the present. It covers habits, routines, general truths, and professions:

- **मैं सुबह जल्दी उठता हूँ।** (Maiṅ subah jaldī uṭhtā hūṅ.) — I get up early in the morning.
- **वह स्कूल में पढ़ाती है।** (Vo skūl meṅ paṛhātī hai.) — She teaches in a school. (पढ़ाना paṛhānā = to teach — note the long ā: पढ़ना is "to read/study," पढ़ाना is "to make read," i.e., teach.)
- **हम रोज़ टहलते हैं।** (Ham roz ṭahalte haiṅ.) — We walk every day.
- **सूरज पूर्व से निकलता है।** (Sūraj pūrv se nikaltā hai.) — The sun rises in the east. (General truths use this form too.)

The ending agrees with the subject: -tā (m. sg.), -tī (f.), -te (pl./respect with masc.; fem. plural keeps -tī: लड़कियाँ खेलती हैं, laṛkiyāṅ kheltī haiṅ).

Frequency words slot in naturally before the verb: रोज़ (roz, daily), अक्सर (aksar, often), कभी-कभी (kabhī-kabhī, sometimes), हमेशा (hameśā, always).

One subtlety: English "I read" can mean habit or right-now; Hindi forces the choice — habitual पढ़ता हूँ for the habit, progressive पढ़ रहा हूँ for this moment. That forced choice, annoying for a week, soon becomes a precision instrument you'll miss in English.
What's the difference between पढ़ता है and पढ़ रहा है? English uses "reads/is reading" loosely.

Hindi doesn't let you be loose here — the two forms answer different questions.

**पढ़ता है (paṛhtā hai)** — habitual: what he *does*, in general.
**वह रोज़ अख़बार पढ़ता है।** (Vo roz akhbār paṛhtā hai.) — He reads the newspaper every day. (Not necessarily now.)

**पढ़ रहा है (paṛh rahā hai)** — progressive: what he is *doing at this moment*. Built from the verb stem + रहा/रही/रहे (rahā/rahī/rahe) + होना:
**श्श! वह अभी पढ़ रहा है।** (Vo abhī paṛh rahā hai.) — Shh! He's studying right now.

The रहा piece agrees in gender too: **वह पढ़ रही है** (she is reading), **वे पढ़ रहे हैं** (they are reading).

Where English actively misleads you:

- "I'm working on it" (right now) → progressive: **मैं उस पर काम कर रहा हूँ।**
- "I work in a bank" (my job) → habitual: **मैं बैंक में काम करता हूँ।** Saying कर रहा हूँ here claims you're at your desk this second.
- States don't take the progressive: "I know" is **मुझे मालूम है / मैं जानता हूँ**, never *जान रहा हूँ — knowing isn't an action in progress.

And a third sibling for completed-and-relevant events: **वह पढ़ चुका है** (vo paṛh cukā hai — he has finished reading), with चुकना (cuknā). Habit, in-progress, done-and-dusted: Hindi makes you pick one of three where English happily blurs.
How does the simple past work for verbs like "went" and "came"?

For **intransitive** verbs (no object — go, come, sit, sleep), the simple past is beautifully plain: the verb stem grows a gender ending, and *no auxiliary is needed*.

- **वह गया।** (Vo gayā.) — He went.
- **वह गई।** (Vo gaī.) — She went.
- **वे गए।** (Ve gaye.) — They went. (fem. pl.: **वे गईं**, ve gaīṅ)
- **मैं कल देर से आया।** (Maiṅ kal der se āyā.) — I (m.) came late yesterday. A woman: **आई** (āī).
- **बच्चा सो गया।** (Baccā so gayā.) — The child fell asleep.
- **बारिश हुई।** (Bāriś huī.) — It rained. (होना's past: हुआ/हुई/हुए — बारिश is feminine, hence हुई.)

The pattern: stem + **-ā** (m. sg.), **-ī** (f. sg.), **-e** (m. pl.), **-īṅ** (f. pl.). A few verbs are irregular in the stem itself — जाना gives गया (not *जाया), होना gives हुआ, करना gives किया (kiyā), देना gives दिया (diyā), लेना gives लिया (liyā), पीना gives पिया (piyā). That short irregular list is worth memorizing cold; everything else is regular.

Important boundary: this clean pattern is for verbs *without* a direct object. The moment a past-tense verb has an object — "I ate **food**," "she read **the book**" — Hindi flips its agreement system entirely (the famous ने construction). That's the next boss fight, and it's genuinely learnable.
OK, the famous one: why does "I ate food" need ने, and why does the verb stop agreeing with "I"?

This is **split ergativity**, and Hindi learners worldwide have wrestled it — so let's build it slowly. In the **past tense of a transitive verb** (a verb with a direct object), three things happen at once:

1. The subject takes the postposition **ने (ne)**.
2. The verb *stops* agreeing with the subject.
3. The verb agrees with the **object** instead.

- **मैंने खाना खाया।** (Maiṅne khānā khāyā.) — I ate food. खाना (food) is masculine → खाया, whether the eater is a man or a woman.
- **लड़की ने किताब पढ़ी।** (Laṛkī ne kitāb paṛhī.) — The girl read the book. किताब is feminine → पढ़ी. The girl's gender is nowhere in the verb.
- **राम ने दरवाज़ा खोला।** (Rām ne darvāzā kholā.) — Ram opened the door. दरवाज़ा masc. → खोला.

Now the contrast that proves the rule — intransitive past has **no ने** and normal agreement:

- **मैं गया।** (Maiṅ gayā.) — I (m.) went. / **मैं गई।** (Maiṅ gaī.) — I (f.) went. No object, no ने, verb agrees with मैं.

Why would a language do this? The deep logic: ने marks the subject as an *agent acting on something*, and the sentence then centers on the thing affected — the verb dresses to match the patient. English speakers find it alien for a month and then automatic.

Two escape hatches to know now: ने appears **only** in perfective (completed) past transitives — never in present or future: **मैं खाना खाता हूँ** (habitual, no ने), **मैं खाना खाऊँगा** (future, no ने). And a handful of verbs — notably बोलना (bolnā, to speak) and often लाना (lānā, to bring) in casual speech — skip ने: **वह बोला** (vo bolā, he spoke).
In the ने construction, what happens when the object has को on it? I heard the verb "gives up" agreeing.

Exactly right — the verb gives up and falls back to a default. When the object is marked with **को (ko)** — which happens when the object is a specific person or a definite, particular thing — the verb can't agree with it (को blocks agreement — a को-marked noun can't control the verb). So the verb takes the **default masculine singular** form, no matter who did what to whom:

- **मैंने लड़की को देखा।** (Maiṅne laṛkī ko dekhā.) — I saw the girl. देखा is masc. sg. — it agrees with *nothing*; it's the fallback. लड़की being feminine changes nothing.
- **उसने मुझे बुलाया।** (Usne mujhe bulāyā.) — He/She called me. बुलाया stays default even if the caller is a woman and "me" is a woman.
- **राम ने चोर को पकड़ा।** (Rām ne cor ko pakaṛā.) — Ram caught the thief.

Compare the trio, and the whole system snaps into focus:

1. **राम ने किताब पढ़ी।** — object bare & feminine → verb feminine (पढ़ी).
2. **राम ने लड़की को देखा।** — object को-marked → verb default masc. (देखा).
3. **राम सो गया।** — no object at all → verb agrees with subject (गया, and a female subject would give गई).

When does को attach? Animate, specific objects almost always take it (people, pets, named things); inanimate objects take it when definite and specific — *the* particular book you both know about, not books in general. **मैंने किताब पढ़ी** (I read a/the book — book as material) vs **मैंने किताब को पढ़ा** (I read *that particular* book — को forces the default पढ़ा). Note that with पढ़ना, speakers usually leave inanimate objects bare; को with things is rarer than with people. Rule of thumb: people get को, things usually don't, and the verb's ending tells you which choice was made.
What are "compound verbs" like खा लिया and दे दिया? Why two verbs?

A compound verb pairs a **main verb** (which carries the meaning) with a **vector verb** (which carries the *flavor* — completion, direction of benefit, suddenness). The main verb appears as its bare stem; the vector conjugates. English does a pale version with "eat *up*," "give *away*" — Hindi grammaticalized it.

The big four vectors:

- **लेना (lenā, take)** — the action is done completely, and the benefit lands on the doer: **मैंने खाना खा लिया।** (Maiṅne khānā khā liyā.) — I ate (it all) up. **उसने किताब पढ़ ली।** (Usne kitāb paṛh lī.) — She read the book through. (Note पढ़ ली agrees with किताब — the ने rules still apply to the vector.)
- **देना (denā, give)** — the action moves *away* from the doer, for someone else: **उसने मुझे किताब दे दी।** (Usne mujhe kitāb de dī.) — She gave me the book (handed it over, done).
- **जाना (jānā, go)** — a change of state, often involuntary or complete: **वह सो गया।** (Vo so gayā.) — He fell asleep. **मैं भूल गया।** (Maiṅ bhūl gayā.) — I (clean) forgot.
- **पड़ना (paṛnā, fall)** — suddenness, bursting out: **बच्चा रो पड़ा।** (Baccā ro paṛā.) — The child burst into tears. And **डालना (ḍālnā, pour/throw)** adds force or thoroughness: **उसने काम कर डाला** (usne kām kar ḍālā — he got the whole job done, forcefully).

Plain खाया says "ate." खा लिया says "ate it all up, for myself, finished." That nuance-per-syllable is why compounds saturate spoken Hindi — roughly every third verb in natural conversation carries one. Learn खाया first, then let लिया/दिया in within the month.
How do I talk about the future — "I will go," "she will come"?

The future tense is a single suffix set glued to the verb stem, agreeing in gender and number — no auxiliary needed:

- **मैं कल जाऊँगा।** (Maiṅ kal jāūṅgā.) — I (m.) will go tomorrow. A woman: **जाऊँगी** (jāūṅgī).
- **वह आएगा।** (Vo āegā.) — He will come. / **वह आएगी।** (Vo āegī.) — She will come.
- **हम साथ चलेंगे।** (Ham sāth caleṅge.) — We will go together.
- **तुम कब आओगे?** (Tum kab āoge?) — When (m.) will you come? To a woman: **आओगी** (āogī).
- **आप कब आएँगे?** (Āp kab āeṅge?) — When will you (respectful) come?

The endings: -ūṅgā/-ūṅgī (I), -egā/-egī (he/she), -oge/-ogī (tum), -eṅge/-eṅgī (we/they/āp). Two stems bend: करना → **करेगा** (karegā, will do), होना → **होगा** (hogā). And कल (kal) does double duty — it means both *tomorrow* and *yesterday*; the verb tense tells you which: **कल जाऊँगा** (will go → tomorrow), **कल गया** (went → yesterday). Hindi speakers lean on the verb, not the noun, for time direction.

One usage note: the future also expresses *probability* in the present — **वह घर पर होगा** (vo ghar par hogā) usually means "he's probably at home," not "he will be at home." Same form, and context separates them, exactly like English "that'll be the postman."
How do wishes and "I need/want" work — I keep hearing चाहिए everywhere.

Two systems here: the subjunctive for wishes and possibilities, and चाहिए for needs and wants.

**The subjunctive** is the bare stem + personal endings (-ūṅ, -e, -o, -eṅ), used after words of wishing, doubt, and purpose:

- **शायद वह आए।** (Śāyad vo āe.) — Maybe he'll come.
- **मैं चाहता हूँ कि तुम खुश रहो।** (Maiṅ cāhtā hūṅ ki tum khuś raho.) — I want you to be happy. (रहो is subjunctive after कि.)
- **काश मैं वहाँ होता!** (Kāś maiṅ vahāṅ hotā!) — If only I were there! (काश kāś + subjunctive/imperfect is the wishing formula.)
- **भगवान करे, सब ठीक हो।** (Bhagvān kare, sab ṭhīk ho.) — God willing, may everything be fine.

**चाहिए (cāhiye)** — "is needed / should" — works with the person in the को form (मुझे, तुम्हें, उसे) and the thing needed as subject:

- **मुझे पानी चाहिए।** (Mujhe pānī cāhiye.) — I need water.
- **मुझे दो टिकट चाहिए।** (Mujhe do ṭikaṭ cāhiye.) — I need two tickets. (चाहिए doesn't change for plural things in modern usage.)
- **तुम्हें आराम करना चाहिए।** (Tumheṅ ārām karnā cāhiye.) — You should rest. (With an infinitive verb: "it is needed that you rest" = advice.)

Distinguish चाहिए from चाहता: **मैं चाय चाहता हूँ** (maiṅ cāy cāhtā hūṅ) is "I *want* tea" — a desire, with the wanter as subject. **मुझे चाय चाहिए** is "tea is *needed* by me" — cooler, more like ordering or stating a requirement. In a restaurant, चाहिए is the natural register; चाहता sounds like a confession. And in the past: **मुझे पानी चाहिए था** (cāhiye thā — I needed water).
कल आपने क्या किया? मुझे सरल हिंदी में बताइए।

ठीक है, मैं कल की बात बताता हूँ। ध्यान दें — मैं "मैं" हूँ, इसलिए क्रियाएँ masculine हैं।

**कल मैं सुबह जल्दी उठा।** (Kal maiṅ subah jaldī uṭhā.) — मैं सुबह छह बजे उठा। मैंने चाय बनाई।
*देखिए — "बनाई" चाय (feminine) से मिली है, मुझसे नहीं! बनाना transitive है, इसलिए "मैंने" आया और क्रिया वस्तु से मिली। यही "ने" का नियम है।*

**फिर मैं बाज़ार गया।** (Phir maiṅ bāzār gayā.) — जाना intransitive है, इसलिए "ने" नहीं आया और क्रिया मुझसे मिली: गया।

**मैंने वहाँ से सब्ज़ी और फल ख़रीदे।** (Maiṅne vahāṅ se sabzī aur phal kharīde.) — ख़रीदना transitive है, इसलिए "मैंने"। और क्रिया? फल और सब्ज़ी मिलकर plural हैं, इसलिए "ख़रीदे"।

**शाम को मैंने एक किताब पढ़ी।** (Śām ko maiṅne ek kitāb paṛhī.) — किताब feminine है, इसलिए पढ़ी।

**रात को मैं जल्दी सो गया।** (Rāt ko maiṅ jaldī so gayā.) — सोना intransitive, इसलिए गया मुझसे मिला।

याद रखें: **वस्तु (object) है तो "ने", और क्रिया वस्तु से मिलती है। वस्तु नहीं है तो क्रिया कर्ता (subject) से मिलती है।**
*(Yād rakheṅ: vastu hai to "ne", aur kriyā vastu se miltī hai. Vastu nahīṅ hai to kriyā kartā se miltī hai.)*
Every Hindi noun is masculine or feminine? Is there any way to guess?

Every noun has a gender, and there *is* a guessing system — it's about 80% reliable, which makes it a strategy, not a rule. Learn the heuristic, then learn its famous traitors.

**The heuristic (word endings):**

- Nouns ending in **-ā** are usually **masculine**: लड़का (laṛkā, boy), कमरा (kamrā, room), दरवाज़ा (darvāzā, door), केला (kelā, banana).
- Nouns ending in **-ī** are usually **feminine**: लड़की (laṛkī, girl), कुर्सी (kursī, chair), खिड़की (khiṛkī, window), चाबी (cābī, key).

**The famous traitors — memorize these on sight:**

- **पानी (pānī, water) — masculine!** पानी ठंडा है (pānī ṭhaṇḍā hai — the water is cold), never *ठंडी.
- **आदमी (ādmī, man/person) — masculine**, despite the -ī.
- **दोस्त (dost, friend) — masculine** by default even for female friends in everyday usage (मेरा दोस्त for a male friend; a woman friend is often मेरी दोस्त in careful usage — usage varies; दोस्त as a word leans masculine).
- **किताब (kitāb, book) — feminine**, no ending clue at all (it's an Arabic loan): किताब अच्छी है।
- **कविता (kavitā, poem) — feminine**, despite ending in -ā.
- **मौसम (mausam, weather) — masculine**; **ख़बर (khabar, news) — feminine**; **दुनिया (duniyā, world) — feminine**; **दिल (dil, heart) — masculine**.

**The survival method:** never learn a noun naked. Learn it inside a gender-revealing frame — यह किताब अच्छी है, मेरा कमरा — so the adjective and possessive teach the gender along with the word. Dictionaries mark m./f.; your notebook should too. And a mercy rule: when genuinely unsure mid-conversation, masculine is the more common default guess for objects — but for the top 200 nouns, just learn them.
How do adjectives change for gender? Is it just अच्छा/अच्छी?

Adjectives ending in **-ā** follow the exact -ā/-ī/-e melody you've seen in verbs:

- **अच्छा लड़का** (acchā laṛkā) — a good boy (m. sg.)
- **अच्छी लड़की** (acchī laṛkī) — a good girl (f., sg. or pl.)
- **अच्छे लड़के** (acche laṛke) — good boys (m. pl.)
- **अच्छे लड़के को** (acche laṛke ko) — to the good boy (m. sg. *oblique* — before a postposition, masculine singular also becomes -e!)

That last line is the one learners miss: masculine -ā adjectives become **-e** not only in the plural but also in the singular oblique case: बड़े कमरे में (baṛe kamre meṅ, in the big room).

More of the family: बड़ा/बड़ी/बड़े (big), छोटा (small), नया (new), पुराना (old), लंबा (tall/long), काला (black), गोरा (fair-skinned), ठंडा (cold), ताज़ा (fresh).

**But a large class never changes at all** — adjectives not ending in -ā are invariable:

- **तेज़** (tez, fast/sharp): तेज़ लड़का, तेज़ लड़की, तेज़ गाड़ी — same तेज़ everywhere.
- **साफ़** (sāf, clean), **ख़राब** (kharāb, bad/broken), **गर्म** (garm, hot), **सुंदर** (sundar, beautiful), **ठीक** (ṭhīk, okay).

Quick diagnostic: if the dictionary form ends in -ā, it dances; if not, it stands still. **यह गाड़ी तेज़ है** (yah gāṛī tez hai) and **यह लड़का तेज़ है** — तेज़ never blinks.
Plurals look chaotic — लड़का becomes लड़के but also लड़कों? What's the system?

There are exactly two plural shapes per noun, and the chaos dissolves once you see why: Hindi nouns inflect for **direct** case (subject/plain object) and **oblique** case (before any postposition). The plural oblique always ends in **-ओं (-oṅ)**.

**Masculine -ā nouns** (the changers): लड़का → **लड़के** (laṛke, direct pl.) → **लड़कों** (laṛkoṅ, oblique pl.)

- लड़के खेल रहे हैं। (The boys are playing.)
- लड़कों को बुलाओ। (Call the boys. — को forces oblique.)

**Masculine consonant-ending nouns** (the stand-stills): घर (ghar, house) → **घर** (direct pl., unchanged) → **घरों** (gharoṅ, oblique).

- दो घर हैं। (There are two houses.) / घरों में (in the houses)

**Feminine -ī nouns**: लड़की → **लड़कियाँ** (laṛkiyāṅ, direct) → **लड़कियों** (laṛkiyoṅ, oblique).

**Feminine consonant nouns**: किताब → **किताबें** (kitābeṅ, direct) → **किताबों** (kitāboṅ, oblique). रात → रातें/रातों (nights).

So every noun's plural is: *direct form* for plain use, *-oṅ form* before में/को/से/पर. Singular oblique matters too — लड़का becomes लड़के even in the singular before a postposition (लड़के को, to the boy), while घर stays घर (घर में). If you learn each plural pair as "the plain one and the -oṅ one," you've learned the whole system; there is no third drawer.
Why does लड़का turn into लड़के in "लड़के को" if there's only one boy?

Because **को doesn't care about number — it demands the oblique case**, and the masculine -ā noun's oblique singular happens to look identical to its direct plural. Two different forms wearing one coat:

- **लड़के खेल रहे हैं।** — लड़के = plural, direct: "The boys are playing."
- **लड़के को बुलाओ।** — लड़के = singular, oblique: "Call the boy."

How do you tell them apart in the wild? The verb and context: खेल रहे **हैं** (plural auxiliary) vs a singular command with one boy in view. Native speakers never confuse them; the grammar around the word disambiguates.

The full oblique picture for masculine -ā nouns: singular oblique लड़के, plural oblique लड़कों. Before every postposition — को, से, में, पर, के लिए — the noun must stand in oblique: **इस लड़के से** (is laṛke se, from this boy), **उस कमरे में** (us kamre meṅ, in that room).

Other noun types in singular oblique:

- Masculine consonant nouns **don't change**: घर में (ghar meṅ), दोस्त से (dost se).
- Feminine nouns **don't change** in the singular oblique: लड़की को (laṛkī ko), किताब में (kitāb meṅ).
- **Pronouns change completely** (suppletive forms): मैं → मुझ (मुझे), वह → उस (उसे/उसको), यह → इस (इसे/इसको).

So the oblique is really one rule with a small footprint: only -ā masculines bend in the singular, everything bends (to -oṅ) in the plural, and pronouns have their own fused forms. Small footprint, constant use — worth drilling early.
Give me a reference table for adjective agreement and noun plurals together — I want the whole gender system on one card.

The gender machine, on one card. Everything in Hindi that can agree uses the same three-way melody: **-ā** (m. sg. direct), **-ī** (f.), **-e** (m. pl. direct + all masculine oblique).

**Adjectives in -ā** (example: बड़ा baṛā, big):

| | masculine | feminine |
|---|---|---|
| sg. direct | बड़ा कमरा (baṛā kamrā, big room) | बड़ी खिड़की (baṛī khiṛkī, big window) |
| sg. oblique | बड़े कमरे में (baṛe kamre meṅ) | बड़ी खिड़की में (baṛī khiṛkī meṅ — unchanged) |
| pl. direct | बड़े कमरे (baṛe kamre) | बड़ी खिड़कियाँ (baṛī khiṛkiyāṅ) |
| pl. oblique | बड़े कमरों में (baṛe kamroṅ meṅ) | बड़ी खिड़कियों में (baṛī khiṛkiyoṅ meṅ) |

Adjectives not ending in -ā never change: तेज़, साफ़, गर्म, ख़राब, सुंदर.

**Noun plurals:**

| noun type | direct plural | oblique plural |
|---|---|---|
| masc. -ā: लड़का (boy) | लड़के (laṛke) | लड़कों (laṛkoṅ) |
| masc. consonant: घर (house) | घर (ghar) | घरों (gharoṅ) |
| fem. -ī: लड़की (girl) | लड़कियाँ (laṛkiyāṅ) | लड़कियों (laṛkiyoṅ) |
| fem. consonant: किताब (book) | किताबें (kitābeṅ) | किताबों (kitāboṅ) |

**Verb agreement mirrors it:** पढ़ता (m.) / पढ़ती (f.) / पढ़ते (m. pl.) / पढ़ती हैं (f. pl. — participle stays -tī, auxiliary हैं).

Memorize the card and you've outsourced 90% of Hindi agreement to one pattern: the -ā/-ī/-e melody, oblique -oṅ plurals, feminine singular oblique unchanged.
For objects, gender seems random. Any anchors for the everyday words?

Gender for things is mostly arbitrary — German and French learners will feel at home — but the highest-frequency words can simply be learned as a fixed cast. Here are twenty anchors, in the phrases you'll actually say them:

**Masculine:** कमरा (kamrā, room) — कमरा बड़ा है। · दरवाज़ा (darvāzā, door) — दरवाज़ा बंद है। (band, closed) · पानी (pānī, water) — पानी ठंडा है। · दूध (dūdh, milk) — यह दूध ताज़ा है। (ताज़ा tāzā shows the masc. -ā; गर्म "hot" is invariable, so it can't prove gender.) · खाना (khānā, food) — खाना तैयार है। · पैसा (paisā, money) — पैसा कहाँ है? · दिल (dil, heart) — मेरा दिल। · मौसम (mausam, weather) — मौसम अच्छा है। · स्कूल (skūl) — मेरा स्कूल। · बाज़ार (bāzār, market) — बाज़ार दूर है।

**Feminine:** किताब (kitāb, book) — किताब अच्छी है। · चाबी (cābī, key) — चाबी कहाँ है? · खिड़की (khiṛkī, window) — खिड़की खुली है। (khulī, open) · गाड़ी (gāṛī, car/train) — गाड़ी नई है। · चाय (cāy, tea) — यह चाय मीठी है। (mīṭhī, sweet — shows feminine.) · कुर्सी (kursī, chair) — मेरी कुर्सी। · मेज़ (mez, table) — मेरी मेज़। · घड़ी (ghaṛī, watch/clock) — मेरी घड़ी। (the possessive shows feminine; ठीक is invariable.) · रोटी (roṭī, flatbread) — रोटी ताज़ी है। (tāzī, fresh — fem.) · बारिश (bāriś, rain) — बारिश हो रही है। (हो रही — the verb shows feminine!)

The trick embedded above: when an adjective is invariable (गर्म, ठीक), let a *changing* word carry the gender — a verb (हो रही है), a possessive (मेरी/मेरा), or a variable adjective (ताज़ा/ताज़ी). Learn each noun holding hands with one such word and the gender sticks.
Why do people use plural verbs for one respected person, like "पिताजी आए हैं"?

Because in Hindi grammar, **plural is the uniform of respect**. A respected singular person — a parent, a teacher, an elder, a guest of honor — takes plural verb forms and the pronoun वे (ve):

- **मेरे पिताजी आए हैं।** (Mere pitājī āe haiṅ.) — My father has come. (आए + हैं — masculine plural forms for one man.)
- **माताजी बैठी हैं।** (Mātājī baiṭhī haiṅ.) — Mother is seated. (बैठी is feminine singular participle; the plural lives in हैं. For a completed past: **माताजी आईं** — āīṅ, the feminine respect-plural ending.)
- **गुरुजी कल पढ़ाएँगे।** (Gurujī kal paṛhāeṅge.) — The teacher will teach tomorrow. (-eṅge respect future.)

The same logic powers **आप**: आप is grammatically plural — **आप कैसे हैं?** — even to one person. And the pronoun **वह** upgrades to **वे** for respected third persons: about your grandfather you say **वे रोज़ सुबह टहलते हैं** (ve roz subah ṭahalte haiṅ — he walks every morning), with plural टहलते हैं.

Where learners slip: mixing levels inside one sentence — *पिताजी आया है (singular verb) sounds like talking about a child or a peer. Pick the respect level at the door and let every verb in the sentence wear it. Hindi listeners register a slipped level the way English listeners register calling the boss "dude" — small slip, loud signal.
मुझे हमेशा गड़बड़ होती है — "किताब अच्छा है" या "किताब अच्छी है"?

कोई बात नहीं — यह हर सीखने वाले की समस्या है। सही है: **किताब अच्छी है।**

कारण सरल है: **किताब स्त्रीलिंग (feminine) है।** इसलिए विशेषण (adjective) भी स्त्रीलिंग होगा — अच्छा नहीं, **अच्छी**।

और उदाहरण देखें:
- **किताब अच्छी है।** (Kitāb acchī hai.) — किताब feminine, इसलिए अच्छी।
- **कमरा बड़ा है।** (Kamrā baṛā hai.) — कमरा masculine, इसलिए बड़ा।
- **खिड़की खुली है।** (Khiṛkī khulī hai.) — खिड़की feminine, इसलिए खुली।
- **दरवाज़ा बंद है।** (Darvāzā band hai.) — दरवाज़ा masculine, इसलिए बंद (बंद बदलता नहीं, यह invariable है)।

याद रखने की तरकीब: नया शब्द सीखते समय उसे अकेला न सीखें। हमेशा एक छोटे वाक्य के साथ सीखें:
- यह **किताब अच्छी** है → किताब = feminine
- यह **कमरा बड़ा** है → कमरा = masculine

एक और जाल (trap): **पानी masculine है** — पानी ठंडा है, ठंडी नहीं! शब्द "-ī" पर ख़त्म हो, तो भी हमेशा feminine नहीं होता।
*(Ek aur jāl: pānī masculine hai — pānī ṭhaṇḍā hai, ṭhaṇḍī nahīṅ!)*
तू, तुम, आप — three words for "you"? Who gets which?

Hindi grades "you" by social altitude, and choosing is a social act, not a grammar detail:

**आप (āp)** — the respectful you. For elders, strangers, officials, teachers, customers, your boss, your in-laws, anyone you'd call "sir/ma'am." Takes plural verbs: **आप कहाँ जा रहे हैं?** Default to आप whenever in doubt — nobody is ever insulted by आप.

**तुम (tum)** — the familiar you. For friends, siblings, juniors, colleagues you're close to, and (in most families) younger relatives. Takes its own verb forms: **तुम कहाँ जा रहे हो?** This is the "default friendly" level of modern urban Hindi.

**तू (tū)** — the intimate/subordinate you. For small children, very close friends in private banter, God in prayer, lovers in poetry and song — and, pointed *downward* at a stranger or subordinate, a deliberate insult. **तू क्या कर रहा है?** said to a stranger can start a fight.

The asymmetry to feel in your bones: the same word that means "my dearest" between friends means "you're beneath me" to a stranger. Context and relationship are everything.

Practical ladder for a learner: आप to everyone new; तुम when they signal closeness (or when they're clearly your age and the setting is casual); तू only when you hear it used *to you* by an intimate — and even then, mirroring it is optional. As a foreigner you'll be forgiven level errors that natives wouldn't be, but आप-first is free insurance.
Why do songs and prayers use तू for God and lovers if तू can be an insult?

Because तू isn't really "rude" — it's **unmediated**. It marks the *absence of social distance*, and that cuts both ways: zero distance can be intimacy or contempt, depending on whether the closeness is mutual.

- **To God:** prayer wants no protocol between the soul and the divine. **तू ही मेरी मंज़िल है** (tū hī merī manzil hai — You alone are my destination) is devotion precisely because तू strips away ceremony. Generations of bhakti and Sufi poetry chose तू for the Beloved for exactly this reason.
- **To lovers in songs:** **तू मेरी ज़िंदगी है** (tū merī zindagī hai — you are my life). The lyric claims a closeness so complete that respect-forms would feel like a wall.
- **Between old friends:** तू with a laugh is a badge — "we're past manners." Friends who grew up together often keep तू for life.
- **To a servant, a stranger, a subordinate who hasn't consented:** the same zero-distance reads as "you don't merit distance" — contempt. This is why तू hurled in an argument lands like a slap.

So the word carries *closeness without consent checks*. Songs and prayers live where closeness is total and mutual. The street asks: is it mutual? When in doubt as a learner, admire तू in lyrics, understand it in films, and let intimates invite you into it. You'll know the invitation when a close friend uses it to you with warmth — that's your green light, for that person only.
How do I give polite commands with आप? "Sit down," "please come," that sort of thing.

With आप, imperatives end in **-इए (-iye)** — and for the highest courtesy, a few verbs have special **-जिए (-jiye)** forms. The ladder for common verbs:

| verb | तुम form | आप form | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| जाना (go) | जाओ (jāo) | **जाइए** (jāiye) | go |
| आना (come) | आओ (āo) | **आइए** (āiye) | come |
| बैठना (sit) | बैठो (baiṭho) | **बैठिए** (baiṭhiye) | sit |
| करना (do) | करो (karo) | **करिए / कीजिए** (kariye / kījiye) | do |
| देना (give) | दो (do) | **दीजिए** (dījiye) | give |
| लेना (take) | लो (lo) | **लीजिए** (lījiye) | take |
| पीना (drink) | पियो (piyo) | **पीजिए** (pījiye) | drink |
| खाना (eat) | खाओ (khāo) | **खाइए** (khāiye) | eat |

In sentences, with कृपया (kṛpayā, please) or ज़रा (zarā, just/a little — the great softener) in front:

- **कृपया बैठिए।** (Kṛpayā baiṭhiye.) — Please sit down.
- **ज़रा इधर आइए।** (Zarā idhar āiye.) — Please come here a moment.
- **यह फ़ॉर्म भरिए।** (Yah fārm bhariye.) — Please fill in this form.

And the future doubles as a courteous command: **आप कल आइएगा** (āp kal āiegā — please do come tomorrow, lit. "you will come") — the -gā ending softens an instruction into an expectation. Offices run on आइएगा/जाइएगा. One warning: never mix levels — आप with a तुम-form verb (आप बैठो) is the grammatical equivalent of "Sir, sit down, dude." Pick आप, take the -इए forms, all the way through the sentence.
What is जी (jī) doing in so many sentences? People keep adding it to my name.

जी (jī) is Hindi's respect particle — a small syllable that adds warmth and deference wherever it lands. It has three main jobs:

**1. After names and titles** — the use you've noticed: **राहुल जी** (Rahul jī), **शर्मा जी**, **माताजी** (mother — the जी is baked in), **गुरुजी** (teacher). It turns a bare name into a respectful address without needing "Mr." It is polite-neutral: used for any adult you respect, regardless of gender.

**2. In answers** — a respectful "yes" upgrade: **जी हाँ** (jī hāṅ, yes certainly), **जी नहीं** (jī nahīṅ), or bare **जी** as "yes / I hear you / pardon?" A shopkeeper's **जी?** means "yes, how can I help?" A listener's soft **जी... जी...** while you talk is aizuchi — "I'm following you."

**3. After kinship and role words** — पिताजी (father), चाचाजी (uncle), दीदी जी... — family terms often carry it permanently.

Tone notes: जी is warm-respectful, never sarcastic by itself, and it softens refusals — **जी, आज नहीं हो पाएगा** (jī, āj nahīṅ ho pāegā — "I'm afraid it won't be possible today") is a gentle no. As a learner, sprinkle जी after the names of elders and teachers and inside your yes-answers; it's the cheapest politeness in the language. One boundary: don't attach it to your *own* name when introducing yourself — जी is given, not self-awarded.
Give me the full ladder of commands — from rude to most polite — for "do it" and "give me".

Hindi commands come in four altitudes, and the same ladder works for nearly every verb. Watch करना (do) and देना (give):

| level | करना (do!) | देना (give!) | used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| तू | **कर** (kar) | **दे** (de) | children, intimates, God — or insults |
| तुम | **करो** (karo) | **दो** (do) | friends, juniors, family |
| आप | **करिए** (kariye) | **दीजिए** (dījiye) | elders, strangers, formal settings |
| आप + softener | **कृपया कीजिए** (kṛpayā kījiye) | **ज़रा दीजिए** (zarā dījiye) | maximum courtesy |

Notice देना and लेना and पीना prefer the -जिए forms (दीजिए, लीजिए, पीजिए) over regular -इए — these are the "irregular-polite" trio, memorized as a set. करना similarly prefers कीजिए in careful speech, though करिए is everywhere.

Softening devices that work at any level:

- **ज़रा (zarā)** before the command: **ज़रा सुनो** (zarā suno — just listen a moment).
- **-ना (-nā) on a तुम command** makes it casual-friendly: **बैठना!** (baiṭhnā — "sit, na!"). Careful, though: the -ना ending imperative (करना, जाना) is the *familiar-casual* imperative, common among friends and in Mumbai speech; it can sound peremptory to elders. Keep it for peers.
- **The future as command**: **तुम कल आओगे** said as an instruction means "you'll come tomorrow" (expectation). For आप: **आइएगा**.

Negative commands swap in मत (commands) — **मत करो** (don't do it, तुम), **मत कीजिए** (आप) — or the softer न with subjunctive in polite requests. Ladder discipline: choose the altitude of your pronoun first; the verb form must match it exactly.
दुकान पर किसी चीज़ के बारे में नम्रता से कैसे पूछें? मुझे कुछ वाक्य चाहिए।

ज़रूर! दुकान पर नम्रता का सबसे आसान तरीक़ा है — **"जी" लगाएँ, "कृपया" कहें, और क्रिया का आप-वाला रूप (जैसे दिखाइए, दीजिए) इस्तेमाल करें।** ये वाक्य सीख लें:

**पूछने के लिए:**
- **जी, यह कितने का है?** (Jī, yah kitne kā hai?) — यह कितने का है, नम्रता से।
- **भाई साहब, ज़रा वह नीली कमीज़ दिखाइए।** (Bhāī sāhab, zarā vo nīlī kamīz dikhāiye.) — Please show me that blue shirt.
- **क्या इससे छोटा साइज़ है?** (Kyā isse choṭā sāiz hai?) — क्या छोटा साइज़ मिलेगा?

**माँगने के लिए:**
- **कृपया एक किलो चीनी दीजिए।** (Kṛpayā ek kilo cīnī dījiye.) — Please give one kilo of sugar.
- **ज़रा वह वाला पैक कीजिए।** (Zarā vo vālā paik kījiye.) — Please pack that one.

**धन्यवाद और विदा:**
- **बहुत-बहुत शुक्रिया।** (Bahut-bahut śukriyā.) — Thank you very much.
- **अच्छा, फिर आऊँगा।** (Acchā, phir āūṅgā.) — Okay, I'll come again.

एक छोटी तरकीब: दुकानदार को **"भाई साहब"** (भाई + साहब) या **"बहन जी"** कहकर बुलाएँ — यह दिल्ली और उत्तर भारत में बहुत आम और नम्र है।
*(Ek choṭī tarkīb: dukāndār ko "bhāī sāhab" yā "bahan jī" kahkar bulāeṅ — yah Dillī aur uttar Bhārat meṅ bahut ām aur namra hai.)*
How do I talk ABOUT a respected woman in the third person? The verb endings confuse me.

A respected woman gets the feminine version of the respect-plural treatment: pronoun **वे (ve)**, plural auxiliaries, and in the past tense the special ending **-ईं (-īṅ)**:

- **वे रोज़ मंदिर जाती हैं।** (Ve roz mandir jātī haiṅ.) — She (respected) goes to the temple daily. जाती (f. sg. participle) + हैं (plural auxiliary).
- **वे कल आईं।** (Ve kal āīṅ.) — She came yesterday. That -ईं is the feminine respect-plural past: आईं, गईं (gaīṅ, went), बैठीं (baiṭhīṅ, sat).
- **वे क्या कह रही हैं?** (Ve kyā kah rahī haiṅ?) — What is she saying?
- **शर्मा मैडम मीटिंग में थीं।** (Śarmā maiḍam mīṭiṅg meṅ thīṅ.) — Mrs. Sharma was in the meeting. (थीं — feminine respect past of होना.)

For a respected man, the parallel set: **वे आए** (ve āe — he came), **वे थे** (ve the — he was), **वे जाते हैं** (ve jāte haiṅ — he goes).

The learner's minefield is consistency: if you open with वे for your grandmother, every verb in the paragraph must stay plural-respectful — **वे आईं और बैठ गईं** (ve āīṅ aur baiṭh gaīṅ — she came and sat down). Dropping mid-story to वह आई demotes her, and Hindi ears notice. Conversely, using वे/आईं for a small child sounds like sarcasm or a joke. Respect grammar is a dial you set per person, per conversation — set it deliberately.
What titles do people actually use — श्री, साहब, मैडम, भाई साहब?

Hindi address is a layered system; here's the working set, from formal paper to street:

**Formal/written:**
- **श्री (Śrī)** — Mr., before a man's name: श्री रमेश गुप्ता. On letters and invitations.
- **श्रीमती (Śrīmatī)** — Mrs., for a married woman; **सुश्री (Suśrī)** is the Ms.-equivalent used in official Hindi; **कुमारी (Kumārī)** for an unmarried woman appears on forms, rarely in speech.
- **महोदय / महोदया (Mahoday/Mahodayā)** — "Sir/Madam" in formal letters, the Hindi of official correspondence.

**Professional/spoken respect:**
- **साहब (Sāhab)** — after names or roles: डॉक्टर साहब, शर्मा साहब. A colonial-era loan that is now simply "respected sir."
- **मैडम (Maiḍam)** — universal for women in offices and shops: शर्मा मैडम.
- **सर (Sar)** — plain English "sir," everywhere in workplaces.

**Street and neighborhood warmth:**
- **भाई साहब (Bhāī sāhab)** — "brother-sir," the default respectful address to a male shopkeeper, driver, or stranger near your age or older.
- **बहन जी (Bahan jī)** — "sister-jī," the parallel for women.
- **बाबूजी, चाचाजी, ताऊजी, दादाजी** — kinship terms extended to elders by age: any grandfather-aged man is दादाजी (grandfather) to the whole street.

Rule of thumb: when you don't know the name, address by *relationship or role + जी/साहब*, never by "excuse me" alone — Hindi expects a person-word. And in a first meeting, let the other person's introduction set the title; mirror what you hear.
ऑफ़िस में बॉस से एक दिन की छुट्टी माँगनी है। नम्रता से कैसे कहूँ?

बॉस से छुट्टी माँगते समय तीन बातें याद रखें: **आप** का इस्तेमाल करें, क्रिया का **-इए** वाला रूप लें, और वजह छोटी और साफ़ बताएँ। यह एक नमूना है:

**नम्र नमूना:**
- **सर, नमस्ते। क्या मैं आपसे एक बात कर सकता हूँ?** (Sar, namaste. Kyā maiṅ āpse ek bāt kar saktā hūṅ?) — पहले इजाज़त माँगें।
- **मुझे कल एक दिन की छुट्टी चाहिए।** (Mujhe kal ek din kī chuṭṭī cāhiye.) — साफ़ माँग।
- **घर पर एक ज़रूरी काम है।** (Ghar par ek zarūrī kām hai.) — छोटी वजह।
- **कृपया मेरी छुट्टी मंज़ूर कीजिए।** (Kṛpayā merī chuṭṭī manzūr kījiye.) — नम्र अनुरोध।
- **बहुत-बहुत धन्यवाद, सर।** (Bahut-bahut dhanyavād, sar.) — अंत में धन्यवाद।

**कुछ और उपयोगी वाक्य:**
- **क्या मैं आज थोड़ा जल्दी जा सकता हूँ?** (Kyā maiṅ āj thoṛā jaldī jā saktā hūṅ?) — क्या मैं जल्दी जा सकता हूँ?
- **मैं अपना काम आज ही पूरा कर दूँगा।** (Maiṅ apnā kām āj hī pūrā kar dūṅgā.) — भरोसा दिलाएँ कि काम रुकेगा नहीं।

ध्यान दें: "मुझे छुट्टी दो" कहना ग़लत होगा — "दो" तुम-स्तर की क्रिया है। बॉस के लिए हमेशा **दीजिए / कीजिए / चाहिए** वाला स्तर रखें।
*(Dhyān deṅ: "mujhe chuṭṭī do" kahnā ġalat hogā — "do" tum-star kī kriyā hai. Bās ke liye hameśā "dījiye / kījiye / cāhiye" vālā star rakheṅ.)*
If someone uses तुम with me, should I use तुम back? How do levels get negotiated?

Usually yes — Hindi levels are **reciprocal among peers and asymmetric across hierarchy**, and the negotiation is mostly silent:

**Peers (same age/status):** symmetric. If a new colleague uses तुम with you warmly, तुम back is the natural mirror; answering with stiff आप can actually create distance — it can read as "I don't want to be close." Among young urban friends, तुम is the default setting, and आप between close friends sounds like a joke or a quarrel.

**Across age/status:** asymmetric by design. Elders may use तुम (or even तू) *down* to you while expecting आप *up* — a grandmother's तुम to you is affection, not an invitation to reply in kind. Bosses vary: some modern offices run on first names and तुम both ways; government and traditional settings keep आप upward.

**The foreigner's special position:** you will receive आप from almost everyone (it's the stranger-default, and also courtesy to a guest), and your own errors are forgiven with unusual generosity. But two signals are worth acting on:

1. An elder who says **"आप नहीं, तुम कहो"** (āp nahīṅ, tum kaho — "not āp, say tum") is giving you a genuine gift of closeness. Accept it — for that person.
2. A friend who suddenly switches from तुम to आप with you is either joking or angry. The level *is* the message.

When truly unsure mid-conversation, match the level used *to* you by the older or higher-status person, and let peers set तुम. The system sounds intricate, but in practice it's one question — "how close are we?" — asked and answered fresh with every person.
नमस्ते vs नमस्कार — and do people really say "good morning" in Hindi?

**नमस्ते (namaste)** is the all-day, all-purpose greeting — hands joined or not, said to one person or a crowd, morning or midnight. It comes from नमः (namaḥ, bowing) + ते (te, to you): "I bow to you." Use it with anyone; it is never wrong.

**नमस्कार (namaskār)** is its more formal elder sibling — same gesture, slightly more ceremony. You'll hear it from newsreaders, on stage, and when addressing a gathering or a very respected person. In daily life, नमस्ते outnumbers it heavily.

**Time-of-day greetings exist but are formal/bookish:** शुभ प्रभात (śubh prabhāt, good morning), शुभ संध्या (śubh sandhyā, good evening), शुभ रात्रि (śubh rātri, good night). They're what textbooks and greeting cards say. What the street actually says at 8 a.m. is... नमस्ते. (English "good morning" is also everywhere in offices and schools — India code-switches greetings freely.)

Regional and religious greetings you'll meet and should recognize:

- **राम-राम (Rām-Rām)** — warm greeting across much of the rural Hindi belt.
- **अस्सलाम अलैकुम (Assalām alaikum)** — Muslim greeting; the reply is **वालैकुम अस्सलाम (Vālaikum assalām)**. Returning it correctly earns real warmth.
- **सत श्री अकाल (Sat śrī akāl)** — the Sikh greeting, common in Punjab and Delhi.

And the everyday opener that isn't a greeting at all: **और बताओ?** (Aur batāo? — "So, tell me — what's up?") between friends, and **कैसे हो? / आप कैसे हैं?** (How are you?) right after the namaste.
मैं पहली बार किसी से मिल रहा हूँ। अपना परिचय हिंदी में कैसे दूँ?

बहुत आसान है! परिचय के लिए ये वाक्य याद कर लें:

**अपना परिचय:**
- **नमस्ते, मेरा नाम डेविड है।** (Namaste, merā nām Ḍeviḍ hai.) — मेरा नाम ... है।
- **मैं अमेरिका से हूँ।** (Maiṅ Amerikā se hūṅ.) — मैं ... से हूँ।
- **मैं दिल्ली में रहता हूँ।** (Maiṅ Dillī meṅ rahtā hūṅ.) — मैं ... में रहता हूँ। (महिला कहें: रहती हूँ।)
- **मैं हिंदी सीख रहा हूँ।** (Maiṅ hindī sīkh rahā hūṅ.) — यह वाक्य सुनकर हर कोई ख़ुश होता है!

**सामने वाले से पूछें:**
- **आपका नाम क्या है?** (Āpkā nām kyā hai?) — आपका नाम?
- **आप कहाँ से हैं?** (Āp kahāṅ se haiṅ?) — आप कहाँ से हैं?
- **आप क्या करते हैं?** (Āp kyā karte haiṅ?) — आप क्या काम करते हैं?

**किसी और का परिचय कराएँ:**
- **ये मेरे दोस्त हैं, राहुल।** (Ye mere dost haiṅ, Rāhul.) — ये मेरे दोस्त हैं।
- **आपसे मिलकर बहुत ख़ुशी हुई।** (Āpse milkar bahut khuśī huī.) — Nice to meet you!

एक छोटी बात: परिचय में हमेशा **आप** से शुरू करें। बाद में दोस्ती बढ़े तो "तुम" अपने आप आ जाएगा।
*(Ek choṭī bāt: paricay meṅ hameśā "āp" se śurū kareṅ. Bād meṅ dostī baṛhe to "tum" apne āp ā jāegā.)*
शुक्रिया or धन्यवाद — which "thank you" do people actually say?

Both are correct; they live in different registers, and choosing between them is a tiny act of style.

**शुक्रिया (śukriyā)** — the everyday word, from Arabic via Urdu. This is what you'll hear ninety times a day: to the driver, the shopkeeper, a friend who passes the salt. Warm it up with बहुत-बहुत (bahut-bahut, many-many): **बहुत-बहुत शुक्रिया।** It feels personal and spoken.

**धन्यवाद (dhanyavād)** — the Sanskritic, formal word. Speeches, letters, announcements, award ceremonies, thank-you notes, and news broadcasts live here: **आप सभी का धन्यवाद।** (Āp sabhī kā dhanyavād — thank you, all of you.) Said to a friend over coffee it sounds like you're delivering an address — affectionately stiff.
